hook.title: At the Table
hook.content: Koffie, thee, een broodje kaas, de rekening: café Dutch is a small script. Bestellen ('to order') and alsjeblieft carry most of the politeness.

pattern.title: Order, eat, ask for the bill
pattern.content: Ik wil koffie, wij drinken thee, ik eet een broodje kaas, de rekening alsjeblieft. The frames are simple; the nouns are the variables.
pattern.trap_note: Een broodje kaas is a cheese roll, not a cheese sandwich on sliced bread; the diminutive is doing real work.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Koffie, Brood & De Rekening):
exercises.target_answer: de koffie, de thee, het broodje, de kaas, de rekening, bestellen
exercises.meaning: coffee, tea, bread roll; sandwich, cheese, bill, to order
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Koffie, Brood & De Rekening": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.
“Ik wil koffie.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Koffie, Brood & De Rekening”.

cues: The pattern: Order, eat, ask for the bill
exercises.explanation: “Wij drinken thee.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Order, eat, ask for the bill.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Een broodje kaas is a cheese roll, not a cheese sandwich on sliced bread; the diminutive is doing real work.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
options: I eat a little bread cheese.
You eat a little bread cheese.
exercises.target_answer: I eat a little bread cheese.
exercises.explanation: “Ik eet een broodje kaas.” is word-for-word “I eat a little bread cheese.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Order, eat, ask for the bill.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.explanation: “De rekening, alsjeblieft.” reuses only material taught in “Koffie, Brood & De Rekening” — Order, eat, ask for the bill.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “De rekening, alsjeblieft.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Order, eat, ask for the bill.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “I order a coffee.”
twist.explanation: Bestellen is the ordering verb; een koffie is the everyday café order.

summary.outcome: Order food and drinks and ask for the bill in Dutch.
summary.takeaway: Café Dutch is a script with a few slots; the politeness lives in alsjeblieft and graag.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: De Trein & Het Ticket.

koffie.etymology_derivation: The same loan chain as English coffee, through Dutch.

thee.etymology_derivation: The same Hokkien source as English tea, borrowed through Dutch.

broodje.etymology_derivation: Diminutive of brood; every diminutive is het.

kaas.etymology_derivation: From Latin cāseus; English cheese palatalized the k, Dutch kept it.

rekening.etymology_derivation: English reckoning and Dutch rekening are the same noun; Dutch narrowed it to bill.

bestellen.etymology_derivation: A prefixed verb; the German cognate bestellen means to order too.
